title: A temporary income boost can become a durable purchase and a future loan obligation
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35026, using variation from the 2008 Economic Stimulus Act to estimate household durable-goods spending and vehicle financing responses
geography: United States; households and consumer expenditures exposed to the 2008 stimulus payment, with vehicle-financing response estimates

observations.period: Within three months of the 2008 stimulus payment

denominator.unit: households in the study's Consumer Expenditure Survey and stimulus-payment variation; exact analytic denominator not disclosed in the bounded extraction

durable_spending.value: households spent about 80% of the stimulus payment on durable goods
durable_spending.unit: estimated share of stimulus payment spent on durables within three months

vehicle_share.value: most of the durable-goods response was on motor vehicles

smaller_durables.value: about 20% of the total durable response was on smaller items

observations.method: The study uses variation from the Economic Stimulus Act of 2008 to estimate how a transitory income shock affected durable-goods spending.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate identifies a spending response, not whether the purchase was necessary, affordable, welfare-improving, or protective of work and care access.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households in the study's expenditure data; detailed subgroup and purchase-need mechanisms are not extracted here.
observations.counterinterpretation: A durable purchase can replace a failing essential, reduce travel or repair costs, or preserve work access; high spending is not automatically overconsumption.

observations.period: Motor-vehicle purchases following the stimulus payment

denominator.unit: households with estimated vehicle response; exact financing denominator not disclosed in the bounded extraction

vehicle_financing.value: the average household borrowed about 40 cents per dollar of stimulus to purchase motor vehicles
vehicle_financing.unit: vehicle-loan leverage relative to stimulus dollars

purchase_form.value: vehicles were often financed, used, or both

future_obligation.value: loan payment, interest, insurance, fuel, repairs, and later resale were not measured in the bounded extraction

observations.method: Study decomposition of the vehicle response and associated financing using consumer-expenditure and vehicle-financing information.
observations.uncertainty: The 40-cent leverage estimate is an average response and does not reveal loan terms, delinquency, repayment burden, or how borrowing differed by income or credit access.
observations.subgroup: Households purchasing motor vehicles in the study period; no same-household later repayment panel is used here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Borrowing can spread a necessary cost over time and provide mobility; the same loan can also reduce later cash margin if income or vehicle costs change.

observations.period: Conversion boundary from temporary income to durable household room

denominator.unit: study-defined transitory-income shock to durable-purchase conversion route

observed.value: payment receipt, durable spending, vehicle purchases, and average vehicle-loan leverage

open.value: purchase need, work or care access, monthly payment, delinquency, repair, insurance, fuel, cash buffer, and later household security

observations.method: Structured extraction of the paper's measured conversion stages and explicit separation of later household outcomes not established by the abstract or bounded review.
observations.uncertainty: The 2008 policy and vehicle market are unusual; the route should not be treated as a universal response to every temporary payment or current financing market.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households in the source-specific expenditure and financing universe.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same observed purchase can be relief, investment, consumption, or future strain depending on the household's need, terms, and later income path.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER PDF used for the paper's abstract and method context.

boundary: This record shows a large durable-spending response to a temporary income shock and substantial vehicle-loan leverage. It does not establish that the purchases improved access, protected work or care, caused later strain, or produced durable household security.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER working-paper PDF used for the extracted findings; Consumer Expenditure Survey microdata and vehicle-financing data are not locally reproduced.
